source.question: e-438
source.value: Calculate $\displaystyle\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \int_2^x \dfrac {t^3} {t-1}\,\textrm d t$ for $x>2.$

decisions.reason: Observed MA content supersedes the stored value

decisions.question: e-438

source.question: e-438
source.value:
The function $\dfrac {t^3} {t-1}$ is continuous on $[2,x],$ where $x>2.$ So FTC II applies, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{2}^{x}\frac{{t}^{3}}{t-1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{x}^{3}}{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: e-439
source.value:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
\displaystyle \int_x^0 \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t  = -  \int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\eqalign{
 \displaystyle\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \int_x^0  \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t 
	& \, \, = \, \, \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \left(-\int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t \right)\
	& \, \, = \, \, -\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \left(\int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t \right)\
	&= \, \, -\dfrac{x^3}{x^2 +1}.}
$$

source.question: e-440
source.value:
To compute $f'(x),$  we first make the substitution $u=x^2$  and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{2}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{2}^{u}\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The integrand is continuous for all $t,$ so by FTC II we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(u) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(u) \\  & =2x\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: e-441
source.value:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $x^2.$

The integrand $t^2 + 2t$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x({u}^{2}+2u) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x(({x}^{2})^{2}+2{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{3} \\  & =2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=x^2,$ as before.

Finally, we can compute $f'(1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =2(1)^{5}+4(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}-2(1) \\  & =2+4-1-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
